10034107:
Heather Pelletier Hermon LD 315
Dear Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,
My name is Heather Pelletier. I am a resident of Hermon and I am the Student Services Coordinator at Maine Vocational Region #4 - United Technologies Center in Bangor.
I am writing today to urge you to vote against LD 315, An Act to Add a Personal Finance Course to the State Graduation Requirements in High Schools. While I agree that personal finance skills are important life skills that Maine graduates should have upon completion of high school, adding it as a graduation requirement is not the best way to achieve this. By adding yet another graduation requirement, students may lose the ability to access critical career and technical education programming through their local CTE Center. Many students that attend CTE schools have difficulty fitting specific graduation requirements into their schedules, and this new requirement would further burden them. As you are aware, career training for high school students is not only gaining in popularity, it is an incredible benefit to the Maine workforce and economy.
As written, the bill will require ALL Maine high school students to take a standalone personal finance course. This is not necessary for students to become proficient in these skills. Personal finance can, and has been, successfully implemented through mathematics and social studies curriculums, as well as embedded into many CTE programs. Please do not create an additional barrier to students accessing their local tech school.
Again, I urge you to reject LD 315.
Thank you for your consideration.
Sincerely,
Heather J. Pelletier, M.Ed. Student Services Coordinator United Technologies Center Bangor, Maine
10034135:
CHAIRS OF THE COMMITTEE ON EDUCATION AND CULTURAL AFFAIRS
LD 315: An Act to Add a Personal Finance Course to the State Graduation Requirements in High Schools
10:00 A.M., Thursday, February 27, 2025 Cross Building, Room 208
IN SUPPORT
Members of the committee, my name is Max Provencher from Prospect, Maine. I am testifying today in strong support of LD 315, a bill that would make personal finance education a guaranteed part of Maine's high school curriculum.
Two years ago, I testified before this committee in support of LD 1284, which sought to require personal finance as a standalone high school course. While that bill ultimately did not become law, the need for this education has only grown stronger. Today, we have another opportunity to ensure that every Maine high school student receives the financial knowledge necessary to make informed decisions about their future.
I graduated from Searsport District High School in 2022 and currently study finance with a concentration in Capital Markets at Bentley University. Attending Bentley has given me a firsthand look at the disparities in financial literacy and career readiness among students, even within the same college environment. Many of my peers who attended well-resourced high schools arrived on campus with a strong foundation in financial concepts, benefiting from structured coursework and personal support networks. This early exposure allows them to navigate career opportunities with confidence, make informed financial decisions, and set long-term goals much earlier.
By contrast, students who did not have access to personal finance education in high school often face a steeper learning curve. Without an understanding of fundamental financial principles--such as credit, investing, and budgeting--they are at a disadvantage when making key decisions about student loans, internships, and career planning. The differences in financial acumen at a young age compound over time, influencing post-graduate success and long-term financial stability. LD 315 ensures that all Maine students, regardless of where they go to high school, are equipped with the knowledge necessary to compete on equal footing in college and beyond.
I know this challenge firsthand. My father, a preschool teacher, was unfamiliar with how to complete the FAFSA, so I had to teach myself how to navigate the process, completing both my section and his. I relied heavily on guidance from the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) to understand the steps, terminology, and requirements. The experience reinforced for me how critical financial education is--not just for students but for families. Without a structured foundation in personal finance, many students are left to figure things out on their own, often making costly mistakes or missing opportunities altogether.
Currently, only 15% of Maine high school students are guaranteed access to a personal finance course. Yet, the benefits of such education are undeniable. Research shows that states with standalone personal

finance requirements see higher credit scores, lower student loan default rates, and improved financial decision-making among young adults. Beyond these measurable impacts, there's another critical factor: opportunity. In states that require personal finance education, students are significantly more likely to participate in business-related extracurriculars, such as FBLA and DECA, which provide invaluable career pathways. Nebraska, a state similar in size to Maine, has both a personal finance requirement and nearly 30 times the student participation in business career and technical organizations.
This is not a partisan issue. LD 315 enjoys overwhelming public support, with 83% of Maine voters in favor of making personal finance a graduation requirement. Furthermore, this bill can be implemented at little to no cost, with curriculum and teacher training support readily available from organizations such as Maine Jump$tart and Next Gen Personal Finance.
Two years ago, I testified with the hope that Maine would join the growing number of states requiring personal finance education. Today, we have another opportunity to do the right thing. By passing LD 315, we can equip the next generation of Mainers with the tools to achieve financial security and independence--regardless of where they go to high school or their family's financial background.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I strongly urge the passage of LD 315.
Max Provencher
10034076:
Melissa Moffett Denbow Jonesport LD 315
I'm writing in support of requiring all high school graduates to have a personal finance course as part of their educational requirements. Everyone needs to have a basic budgeting education in order to have financial success. This life skill should consistently be taught to Maine students, not just in pockets across the state.
The additional requirement would be an easy lift for Maine educators. There are many free resources available. The Maine Jump$tart Coalition is one of those resources. In 2024, the Maine Jump$tart board was honored to be the national coalition of the year in Washington, DC. As a board member, I am proud to be a part of our Maine conference each year, and be able to send the most teachers to the national conference. But to be a true leader for financial health, our education system should mandate that all students have the graduation requirement.
I also am a strong proponent of this requirement as a mother and in my career. I have an FPQP certification, which is a financial paraplanner. In my 30+ year banking career, I have seen too many customers who are unable to purchase a car or their first home due to credit issues. And this all comes down to managing your household budget.
Thank you for allowing me to express my personal opinion on the bill. This requirement will help build strong financial foundations and, in turn, a stronger state of Maine.
10034455:
Sam Scogin Auburn / MEA LD 315
Dear Esteemed Members of the Education Committee,
My name is Sam Scogin and I currently teach at Lewiston High School. I've been an educator for the past twelve years and have taught a version of a Personal Finance course for many of them.
While the high school I work at currently offers a finance course, it was only after many years of pushing the administration and guidance department to prove how necessary the course is for the future of students. Currently, the course is offered as an elective and is not required for all students.
When I have taught finance, students have started my course with career and secondary education exploration. From there, they manage hypothetical finances and navigated the realities of adulthood by finding apartments, understanding a lease, purchasing vehicles, and much more.
It has also allowed me to build close relationships with students around finances. This is something that many families do not know how to navigate or feel uncomfortable navigating.
I have had students change what they wanted to do for a living after taking the class, simply from having the time to consider more carefully what they want out of their lives. I have also had conversations with students about where they want to live, etc. Kids leave my course with a different understanding and approach to money, and many students and parents have checked in years later to express how useful it has been.
Ultimately, having this as part of the required curriculum is about helping kids get ahead quickly and giving them an advantage of not making many of the same mistakes we did when we were younger. Maine needs this change and I hope you are able to act accordingly.
Thank you for your consideration,
-Sam Scogin LHS Social Studies Teacher
10034245:
Support for LD 315: An Act to Add a Personal Finance Course to the State Graduation Requirements in High Schools February 25, 2025
Dear Education and Cultural Affairs Committee,
My name is Sarah Rowland. I live in Augusta and work for the Finance Authority of Maine (FAME) as an Education Programs Specialist. While I am not officially representing FAME with my testimony, I feel my employment there is a relevant factor.
I am writing today in support of LD 315, An Act to Add a Personal Finance Course to the State Graduation Requirements in High Schools. In my work, I help to administer several different student loan products as well as other forms of student financial aid. I have witnessed first-hand as I have worked with students from across the state, that these young adults are often not prepared in a meaningful way to be confident that they are making good financial decisions, especially as it relates to taking out loans to attend college. I often find myself giving students a crash-course on what their loan terms mean, what is expected of them as a responsible borrower, and what differentiates a loan from a scholarship or a grant. Anecdotally, it seems that many of these students have not even been exposed to these concepts before.
Many students go straight from high school to postsecondary education where they (or sometimes their families) take out large loans to pay for their education which they feel is required to be able to secure decent employment without regard for the return on their investment and ultimately find that they struggle to stay afloat while repaying their student loans. This is especially critical given the unstable nature of our economy, as well as possible changes on the federal level to many aid programs that help lower-income populations access higher education.
While FAME puts forth a great effort to help bolster the financial literacy of all Mainers, making personal finance a graduation requirement in Maine will help ensure that all Maine students are aware of concepts like saving, budgeting, and even investing, to help build a more financially-savvy Maine. If we are lucky, those students will take their knowledge home and help spread it to their families and older friends that were not fortunate enough to have the opportunity to learn financial literacy while they were in school.
As written, the bill will guarantee that ALL Maine high school students will benefit from this life-changing instruction, not just the 15% who are already fortunate to have this course as a standalone graduation requirement.
Thank you for your consideration, and I look forward to the successful passage of LD 315.
Sincerely,
Sarah Rowland Education Programs Specialist Finance Authority of Maine
10034078:
Subject: Support for LD 315: Personal Finance Course
Dear Representative Crockett,
Thank you for your public service in Augusta on behalf of House District 112.
I am writing to show to you and all other representatives support for LD 315, "An Act to Add a Personal Finance Course to the State Graduation Requirements in High Schools."
I submitted this testimony both in writing and live two years ago, and I haven't edited much for this occasion. The financial and economic landscape is perhaps the most fragile and challenging we've seen in generations, and it is incomprehensible that anyone in Maine government would oppose basic financial education for all Maine students.
I have been involved with personal finance (PF) education for over 20 years, most of that in Maine. I have taught PF in the classroom along with economics and business, I serve on the board for the Maine Jump$tart Coalition for Personal Financial Education, and I have designed and implemented PF teacher training events in Maine for a decade.
But that overview of experiences is not important compared to what I have learned from my students and their parents over the years. I am not going to break out compelling statistics and surveys that illustrate the need for PF education and the public's overwhelming opinion that it should be a requirement for a high school diploma. All of that is just a click away on the web. Instead, I'm going to offer just a few of the symptoms that prove the disease, a disease for which PF education is the best treatment we have and one that we owe our children.
� Elections are more than ever dominated by economic issues, and our electorate should be able to base their choices on more than just clever TV ads and misleading social media campaigns.
� Rent-to-own stores, same-day lenders and check cashing centers are runaway successful businesses in this country.
� We ask 18-year-olds to make six-figure decisions on financing higher education, but we do not provide the tools needed to responsibly make that decision; and we wonder why there is a student loan crisis.
� The uniformed borrowing decisions of an 18-year-old can lead to a dinged credit score which can lead to 1% more on a mortgage which can cost $100,000 or more over a lifetime.
� The monthly payment mentality is institutionalized and marketed unchecked to our children. � Profit driven social media is now the primary source of PF discussion and information for current
and potentially future generations. � High risk instruments such as cryptocurrencies and NFTs are thought of by young people as
real investments rather than the speculative gambles that they are. � The idea that consumption leads to happiness is a destructive, unfortunate, and omnipresent
characteristic of American life. � This list could go on for pages.
Finally, a sample of the most common feedback I've received from students and parents over the years (I am 100% comfortable saying that other PF teachers would report similarly):
� "I'm 25 years old, debt free, and I just opened a Roth IRA. It would have never happened if I hadn't taken your class."

� "I advised my parents on how to improve their insurance coverage!" � "WHY ISN'T THIS REQUIRED FOR ALL STUDENTS?"
Unfortunately, this is what I hear from folks who did not learn about money while in school:
� "I have $80,000 in student loans and six credit cards and a car loan. Should I get another credit card or take another loan to help me get out of this situation?"
That question should not plague Maine's youth any longer. American capitalism is full of financial opportunity, but it is laced with equal or worse financial peril. I believe in learning history and science, English and the arts. However, none of those core subjects or anything else required for graduation helps prepare students for the realities of predatory lending, out-of-reach housing prices, the uniquely American health insurance quandary, easily accessible debt-building instruments such as credit cards and buy-now/pay-later schemes. How is learning about war and literature critical to our education but learning how to keep a roof over one's head is not?
My education and foundation of thinking is economics-based, so I understand that when we add something, there is a cost, there is a trade-off. Requiring PF education has a cost, whether it's less time to teach something else, longer days or just the costs of instruction. However, the cost of not guaranteeing every Maine student the opportunity for personal financial education is staggering and, ultimately, one paid by everyone across all generations and communities.
Provide schools the time to adapt their curriculums and budgets. Utilize the expertise of organizations like Maine Jump$tart, the Financial Authority of Maine, Next Gen Personal Finance, and others. Task our school officials/administrators with designing a sensible rollout which does not unfairly land on already stretched teachers. Use these strategies and more to overcome obstacles but find a way to make this happen.
How can we justify not taking this step for Maine's high school students based on administrative or political roadblocks?
I am still waiting for a coherent and detailed explanation from the opposition on why Maine's youth are still not guaranteed this critical piece of education.
We owe current and future generations access to the tools they need to thrive under - and sometimes simply survive - America's uniquely complicated and challenging brand of capitalism.
Thank you for your consideration, and I look forward to the successful passage of LD 315.
Best regards,
Steve Kautz Portland, Maine helloskautz@gmail.com 207-239-4542
